title: You are blamed for a failure in front of everyone
lede: In a status meeting with twelve people and your boss's boss on the call, a colleague says: "Well, the delay came from your side." It is not true, or it is a quarter true. Every face turns to your square on the screen.

blocks.text: In a status meeting with twelve people and your boss's boss on the call, a colleague says: "Well, the delay came from your side." It is not true, or it is a quarter true. Every face turns to your square on the screen.

items: You are facing two separate audiences with different needs. The room wants to know whether the project is safe. Your reputation needs the record corrected. If you serve only the second, you look defensive and you lose both.
Detailed self-defence in a public meeting reads as guilt almost regardless of the facts. Length signals anxiety. The person who speaks briefly and factually is heard as the person in control.
Whether the accusation was strategic or careless matters — but not now. Now is for the record. Motive is a conversation for a smaller room.

items.detail: Long enough to unclench your jaw. The first sentence out of an ambushed person is almost always the wrong one.
One sentence with a verifiable fact in it. No adjectives, no tone, no history.
Pivot to what happens next. This hands the room what it actually wants and ends the spectacle without you appearing to flee it.
Never litigate intent publicly. Say you will follow up, and then genuinely do.

items.move: Put the facts in writing within the hour
items.detail: A short, unemotional note to the relevant people with the dates. The written record outlives the meeting's vibe, and vibes are what people misremember.

items.say: "That is not quite the sequence — the spec landed on the 14th and we shipped on the 16th. Happy to walk anyone through the log."
"The more useful question is the delivery date. Here is what I think it takes."
"I do not think we should use everyone's time to reconstruct this. Let's take it after and come back with one answer."
"In the meeting you said the delay came from my side. That was not accurate, and it landed in front of your boss. What happened there?"

items: The long defence with five sub-points. Everyone stops listening at point two and remembers only that you talked a lot.
Counter-blaming in the same breath. The room files you both as unreliable.
Sarcasm and the wounded laugh. Both read as guilt on a recording.
Silence, if the claim is materially false. Unanswered claims harden into the official story within about a week.
The furious all-caps message afterwards, which converts your correct position into an HR matter about your conduct.
Ask the colleague directly and privately what happened. Roughly half the time it is sloppiness, not strategy, and that changes your response entirely.
If it was strategic and repeats, start keeping dated records and stop relying on verbal agreements with that person.
Tell your own manager your version in one paragraph before the meeting reaches them secondhand.
Notice whether the room is one where facts get you protected. If wrong statements stand unchallenged and challenging them costs you, that is information about the organisation.
